chapter_theme: A yogic song at Thiruvennainallur (திருவெண்ணெய்நல்லூர்): the poet asks to burn the tattvas, still the breath and enter the space of Siva and the dance in the golden hall; the praise names Murugan as the poet who impaled the Jains and the old man who came to Valli.

744.reading: The poet describes a yogic ascent: burning the many tattvas, the darkness consumed by fire, stopping the breath and closing the one path so that it runs by the sun's path into the sky until all is Siva, then melting in the golden hall where the dance is done to ringing anklets and sinking in the full sea, ever with Gauri and Hara; he asks for grace that this may come. The praise names Murugan as the young one who won fame as the poet who set the base Jains on stakes in rows, who came to the hunter girl as an old man by the spring and embraced her when the elephant came, and as son of the pure goddess, at Thiruvennainallur by the Pennai where he dances on the peacock.
744.nuance: பவனம் ஒழித்து, stopping the breath, and பருதி வழி, the sun's path, are terms of breath yoga, and சிவமயம் names its end; the song then moves to the dance in கனக சபை, Chidambaram's golden hall. அமணர் உடல்களை நிரையில் கழுக்களில் உறவிடு சித்திர புலவன் identifies Murugan with Sambandar. The goddess lines (குமரி தகப்பனை மழுகொடு வெட்டிய) seem to recall Daksha's punishment, and the last line of the plea (கழிய நலக்கினி நிறமென விற்றுடல்) does not split with certainty.

links.note: Both turn the plea into a yogic programme, breath, the sun's path, the sky and the dance in 744; muladhara, the three mandalas, bindu and nada and the central pillar in 762; and both praise Murugan as the saint who sent the Jains to the stake.
